A kohlrabi is a vegetable. More specifically, it is a plant whose swollen, round stem is the main edible part. It belongs to the same plant family as cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, and Brussels sprouts — a family known for being nutritious and widely eaten around the world.

Most vegetables you eat underground are roots (like carrots) or tubers (like potatoes). Kohlrabi is different — its round, ball-like edible part grows above the ground, sitting right at soil level. This rounded, swollen part is actually a thickened stem, not a root. This makes it a fairly unique-looking vegetable.

Thin stalks with flat leaves grow outward directly from this round stem, giving the whole plant a slightly alien, almost spacecraft-like appearance — like a round ball with antennae sticking out of it.

• Shape: Round, roughly the size of a tennis ball, though it can grow as large as a grapefruit if left in the ground longer.
  • Outer skin color: Either pale green or deep purple, depending on the variety. Both varieties are the same on the inside.
  • Inner flesh: Always pale white or creamy white, regardless of the outer color.
  • Texture: Firm and crisp, much like the thick stem of a broccoli head.
  • Leaves: Green, flat, and edible, sprouting from the sides of the round stem on thin stalks.

Kohlrabi has a mild, slightly sweet flavor. The closest comparison is the taste of a broccoli stem — but milder, a little juicier, and with a very faint hint of pepper. Some people also compare it to a mild turnip or a sweet, delicate cabbage. It is not bitter, not sharp, and not overpowering — it is a gentle, pleasant-tasting vegetable.

When eaten raw, it is crunchy and refreshing. When cooked, it becomes soft and tender, and its sweetness comes out a little more.

Both main parts of the kohlrabi plant are edible:

  1. The round stem (the bulb): This is the primary edible part. The tough outer skin is peeled away first, and the pale flesh inside is what is eaten — raw or cooked.
  2. The leaves: These are also edible and can be cooked in the same way you would cook kale or spinach — sautéed, added to soups, or steamed.
How Is It Used in Cooking?

Kohlrabi is a very flexible vegetable in the kitchen. Here are the common ways it appears:

  • Raw: Peeled and sliced thinly or cut into sticks, it can be eaten as a snack, added to salads, or used in coleslaw for a crunchy texture.
  • Cooked: It can be roasted, steamed, boiled, stir-fried, or added to soups and curries. Heat softens it and brings out a pleasant, natural sweetness.
  • Stuffed: Large kohlrabi bulbs are sometimes hollowed out and stuffed with a filling, then baked — a popular preparation in some European cuisines.
  • Grated: It can be grated and used in fritters or mixed into dishes where a mild, crunchy element is needed.

It is especially common in German, Eastern European, Indian (particularly Kashmiri), and Vietnamese cuisines.
How Does It Fit Into the Vegetable World?

Kohlrabi is classified as a stem vegetable — because the part you mainly eat is a swollen stem. This puts it in an interesting category alongside things like celery (which is also a stem). It is not a root vegetable, not a leafy green, and not a fruit-vegetable like a tomato. It sits in its own neat corner as a swollen, above-ground stem that happens to be delicious.

Kohlrabi is a round, above-ground, stem vegetable with pale green or purple skin and crisp white flesh, mild and slightly sweet in taste, belonging to the cabbage family, and eaten both raw and cooked.
